extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (esp. aesthetics and Kantian studies)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Immanuel Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgement (Introduction and opening sections) that lays out the division of philosophy, the faculties (understanding, judgement, reason), and transcendental principles such as the purposiveness of nature that ground aesthetic and teleological judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Philosophy into theoretical and practical
rubrics_metrics.description: We proceed quite correctly if, as usual, we divide Philosophy ... into theoretical and practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two parts are distinct because the concepts that furnish their objects must be specifically distinct; a valid division presupposes a contrast between the principles of rational cognition belonging to different parts of a science. Theoretical (Natural Philosophy) rests on natural concepts and supplies principles a priori for cognition of nature; Practical (Moral Philosophy) rests on the concept of freedom and supplies fundamental propositions for the determination of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of concepts: natural concepts and the concept of freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only two kinds of concepts ... natural concepts and the concept of freedom. The former render possible theoretical cognition according to principles a priori; the latter supply fundamental practical propositions (the concept of freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural concepts ground theoretical laws; the concept of freedom does not yield theoretical determinations but furnishes practical laws (moral legislation). This distinction is the basis for separating technically practical rules from morally practical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technically practical versus morally practical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the concept determining the causality of the will is a natural concept, the principles are technically practical; if it is a concept of freedom, they are morally practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically practical rules (rules of art, prudence, housekeeping, statesmanship, etc.) are corollaries of theoretical philosophy and are precepts, not laws. Morally practical principles rest solely on the concept of freedom (supersensible) and are properly called laws (they are not sensuously conditioned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Territory vs realm distinction for concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts, so far as they are referred to objects, have their field determined according to the relation that their Object has to our cognitive faculty: the part where knowledge is possible is a territory (territorium); the part where they are legislative is the realm (ditio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical concepts have a territory (dwelling-place) but no realm because their rules are empirical and contingent. The whole cognitive faculty has two realms (natural concepts and concept of freedom) in which it is legislative a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement as a distinct faculty potentially legislating a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement is a faculty distinct from Understanding and Reason and may contain in itself a special principle a priori (even if only subjective a priori).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgement is intermediate: it relates to the application of concepts (Understanding) and to Reason's practical legislation. Because it is tied to the feeling of pleasure/pain, it may provide a principle that enables transition between theoretical and practical spheres; Critique of Judgement is required to investigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant versus reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the universal (rule) is given and the particular is subsumed under it, the Judgement is determinant. If only the particular is given and the universal must be found, the Judgement is reflective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinant Judgement subsumes particulars under universal transcendental laws already provided by the Understanding. Reflective Judgement must ascend from particulars to universals and therefore requires a principle it cannot derive from experience; reflective Judgement gives a law to itself (not to nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the purposiveness of nature (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the purposiveness of nature in its manifoldness: nature is represented as if an Understanding contained the ground of the unity of the manifold of its empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This purposiveness is a transcendental concept a priori originating in Reflective Judgement. It does not ascribe objective purposes to natural objects but serves as a principle for reflecting upon natural products so as to systematize empirical laws into a coherent experience. It is distinct from practical purposiveness (human art or morals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental principle / law of the specification of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judgement has in itself a principle a priori of the possibility of nature, a law of the specification of nature in respect of its empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws appear contingent from the Understanding's perspective, Reflective Judgement prescribes to itself the assumption that a cognisable order of nature according to particular empirical laws is possible—a necessary presupposition for making connected experience and investigating natural variety. This principle is subjective (a maxim) of Judgement, not an objective law laid on nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a transcendental Deduction of purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposiveness of nature for our cognitive faculties is a transcendental principle of judgements and needs a Transcendental Deduction to ground it in the sources of cognition a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims of Judgement (e.g., nature takes the shortest way, makes no leaps, exhibits unity under a few principles) indicate a necessary way of judging not demonstrable from empirical concepts. A Deduction seeks the grounds in a priori capacities that justify using purposiveness as a reflective principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of purposiveness in enabling a unified experience from empirical manifold
rubrics_metrics.description: Because universal laws of Understanding do not determine the specific empirical laws, Judgement must assume a unity (purposiveness) to allow the formation of a system of experience out of manifold contingent empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Understanding requires this presupposed harmony to divide nature into genera/species and to employ principles that explain one species by analogy with another; without assuming purposiveness, investigation and systematic science of empirical nature would not be practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the feeling of pleasure with purposiveness (aesthetic link)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thought harmony of nature in the variety of its particular laws with our need of finding universality must be judged as contingent yet indispensable, and this harmony (purposiveness) is linked to a feeling of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discovery of systematic unity in nature relieves our cognitive needs and is accompanied by pleasure; this links the faculty of knowledge (Understanding) to the faculty of desire (Reason) via feeling (pleasure/pain), situating aesthetic judgement as a mediator between theoretical and practical spheres.
